questions.q: Tourism supply is:
o: The quantity of tourism products that sellers are willing and able to sell
The quantity of tourism products that tourists are willing and able to buy
The number of tourists arriving at a destination
The money tourists spend in a destination
questions.d: Tourism supply: the quantity of tourism products that sellers (suppliers or providers) are willing and able to sell.
questions.w: Supply is about the sellers. The second option is the definition of demand.

questions.q: How is tourism demand measured, according to the slides?
o: By counting the number of visitors or tourists who come to the destination
By counting the number of hotels
By the size of the destination
questions.d: Tourism demand: the quantity of tourism products buyers (tourists) are willing and able to purchase; it needs both willingness and ability.
questions.w: Demand comes from tourists, so it is measured by how many of them arrive.

questions.q: The tourism product is described as composite because it includes:
o: Everything the tourist purchases, sees, experiences and feels from leaving home until returning
Only souvenirs bought at the destination
questions.d: Tourism product: composite in nature, covering everything the tourist purchases, sees, experiences and feels from leaving home until returning.
questions.w: It is a combination of many parts, not a single item.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the 3 A's of the tourism product?
questions.d: The 3 A's: attractions and activities, amenities, accessibility.
questions.w: Advertising helps sell the product but is not one of its components.

questions.q: Amenities are divided into:
questions.d: Amenities: the infrastructure and superstructure at the destination (e.g. roads, utilities, hotels).
questions.w: Natural and man-made describe attractions, not amenities.

questions.q: Accessibility of a destination is affected by:
o: Geographical proximity, cost of transport and frequency of transport
The core values of the destination
questions.d: Accessibility: affected by the destination's geographical proximity, the cost of transport to it and the frequency of transport.
questions.w: Accessibility is about how easy it is to get there.

questions.q: A hotel room left unsold tonight cannot be stored and sold tomorrow. Which characteristic is this?
questions.d: Perishability: services cannot be physically stored.
questions.w: Tonight's unsold room is lost forever, so the product perishes.

questions.q: A tourist must travel to the beach to enjoy it, because the beach cannot be brought to the tourist. Which characteristic is this?
questions.d: Immovability: the tourism product cannot be taken to the consumer.
questions.w: The consumer has to come to the product.

questions.q: A city cannot quickly add hundreds of hotel rooms when demand jumps during a festival. Which characteristic is this?
questions.d: Rigidity of supply: some facilities cannot change quickly in the face of changes in demand.
questions.w: Building capacity takes time, so supply is rigid.

questions.q: The tourism product is made up of many diverse components. Which characteristic is this?
questions.d: Heterogeneity: the product is composed of many diverse components.
questions.w: Transport, accommodation, food and attractions together make one varied product.

questions.q: A visitor attraction is described as:
o: The core component of the tourism product that attracts a person to visit the destination
questions.d: Visitor attraction: the core component of the tourism product at the host destination that attracts people to visit.
questions.w: Without an attraction there is little reason to travel to the destination.

questions.q: Rivers, lakes, beaches, caves, national parks and forests are:
questions.d: Natural attractions (Swarbrooke): rivers, lakes, beaches, caves, scenic features, flora and fauna, national parks, wilderness and forests.
questions.w: They are created by nature, not people.

questions.q: Historic houses, castles and forts that were NOT originally built to attract tourists are:
questions.d: Man-made attractions: not originally designed to attract tourists, e.g. historic houses, castles, heritage and archaeological sites.
questions.w: A fort was built for defence, not tourism, so it is man-made but not purpose-built.

questions.q: Museums, theme parks, aqua-parks, zoos and golf courses are:
o: Man-made attractions not designed for visitors
questions.d: Purpose-built attractions: created with the purpose of attracting visitors.
questions.w: These were built specifically for visitors.

questions.q: How do event attractions differ from other attractions?
o: They occur only periodically and may change venues
questions.d: Event attractions: from small festivals to hallmark events, occurring periodically and sometimes changing venues.
questions.w: Hallmark events (e.g. the Olympics) also need large investment in buildings and infrastructure.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a factor affecting tourism SUPPLY on the slides?
questions.d: Supply factors: natural resources, investment and capital, skilled workforce, government policy, impacts on the host community, host acceptance, accessibility, infrastructure and superstructure.
questions.w: Disposable income is a travel facilitator, which affects demand.

questions.q: Tourism demand is a function of which three factors?
o: Travel facilitators, resistance factors and travel motivators
questions.d: Factors affecting demand: travel facilitators, resistance factors and travel motivators.
questions.w: The 3 A's describe the product (supply), not demand.

questions.q: Which of these is a travel FACILITATOR?
o: Lack of information on the destination
questions.d: Travel facilitators: disposable income, discretionary leisure time, basic tourism services, political stability, accepted mediums of exchange, access to travel documents.
questions.w: The other three options are resistance factors.

questions.q: Which of these is a RESISTANCE factor?
o: Lack of amenities at the destination
questions.d: Resistance factors: political instability, location, cost, health and safety, climate, perceived image, lack of amenities, lack of information.
questions.w: Resistance factors dissuade a person from travelling.

questions.q: What is the difference between travel facilitators and travel motivators?
o: Facilitators predict whether a person CAN travel; motivators explain WHY they travel
Facilitators explain why people travel; motivators predict whether they can
questions.d: Travel facilitators: predictors of ability to travel. Travel motivators: the reasons for travel.
questions.w: Stopping people travelling is the role of resistance factors.

questions.q: Ramumbo's PHYSICAL motivators relate to:
o: Bodily health and reducing stress through physical activity
questions.d: Ramumbo's four motivators: physical, cultural, interpersonal, status and prestige.
questions.w: Physical motivators are about the body: health and stress relief, e.g. tramping.

questions.q: Travelling to enhance one's reputation or self-worth is which Ramumbo motivator?
questions.d: Status and prestige motivators: the need for esteem and recognition.
questions.w: Reputation and self-worth are about esteem.

questions.q: In Gray's theory, the desire to exchange the known for the unknown and explore new places is:
questions.d: Gray: the prime motivation is to escape routine, made of two forces: wanderlust and sunlust.
questions.w: Wandering and exploring is wanderlust.

questions.q: A family travels to a destination mainly for better weather, sun and sand. In Gray's theory this is:
questions.d: Sunlust: a lust for the sun, or for better physical conditions than in the generating market, e.g. 'sun and sand' tourism.
questions.w: The motive is better physical conditions, not exploring the unknown.

questions.q: Travel motivations are often hidden and must be distinguished from the stated purpose of travel.
questions.d: Motivations tend to be covert (hidden) and differ from the stated purpose (e.g. holiday).
questions.w: Two people can both say 'holiday' but have very different reasons.

questions.q: Two people with the same stated purpose of travel must have the same motivation.
questions.d: Same purpose, different reasons: one may escape work stress, the other may want to socialise.
questions.w: Purpose and motivation are different things.

questions.q: Natural attractions are usually in public ownership and need strict management to protect them.
questions.d: Natural attractions are usually publicly owned and demand strict management regimes to protect them from visitors' use.
questions.w: Heavy visitor use can damage fragile natural sites.

questions.q: Hallmark events need considerable investment in buildings, infrastructure, planning and organisation.
questions.d: Hallmark events: major events like the Football World Cup or Olympics, which promote the host destination.
questions.w: They also have to safeguard the health, safety and security of visitors.

questions.q: Facilitators, motivators and resistance factors operate at a general level and a specific level.
questions.d: General level: whether to take a holiday at all. Specific level: which destination, hotel or product.
questions.w: Both decisions are influenced by the same three factors.

questions.q: Cultural motivators relate to the need for esteem and recognition.
questions.d: Cultural motivators: learning about other countries, cultures, arts and traditions.
questions.w: Esteem and recognition are status and prestige motivators.

questions.q: Define the tourism product and explain its components (the 3 A's).
questions.a:
Tourism product: composite in nature; everything the tourist purchases, sees, experiences and feels from leaving home until returning.
1. Attractions and activities: activities, site attractions and event attractions (e.g. natural and archaeological sites).
2. Amenities: infrastructure and superstructure (e.g. roads, utilities, hotels).
3. Accessibility: affected by geographical proximity, cost of transport and frequency of transport to the destination.
questions.d: The 3 A's: attractions and activities, amenities, accessibility.
questions.w: Define the product first, then explain each A with an example.

questions.q: Explain the characteristics of the tourism product.
questions.a:
1. Service orientation: depends on people; the link between the tourist and the service consumed.
2. Perishability: services cannot be physically stored (an unsold room tonight is lost).
3. Rigidity of supply: some facilities cannot change quickly when demand changes.
4. Immovability: the product cannot be taken to the consumer; the tourist must travel to it.
5. Heterogeneity: it is made of many diverse components.
questions.d: Like many services, the tourism product differs from tangible goods.
questions.w: Each characteristic shows a way tourism differs from a physical product you can store and ship.

questions.q: Explain Swarbrooke's (2001) classification of visitor attractions, with examples.
questions.a:
1. Natural attractions: rivers, beaches, caves, national parks, forests; usually publicly owned and strictly managed (e.g. Oman's wadis and beaches).
2. Man-made attractions not built for tourists: historic houses, castles, forts, heritage and archaeological sites (e.g. a historic fort).
3. Man-made, purpose-built attractions: museums, galleries, theme parks, zoos, golf courses, shopping venues (e.g. a national museum).
4. Event attractions: from community festivals to hallmark events (e.g. Football World Cup, Olympics, Formula One); they occur periodically and need large investment.
questions.d: Visitor attraction: the core component of the tourism product that attracts people to a destination.
questions.w: The key difference between types 2 and 3 is whether the place was built to attract visitors.

questions.q: What are the factors affecting tourism supply?
questions.a:
1. Natural resources and attractions at the destination.
2. Levels of investment and availability of capital.
3. Availability of a skilled workforce.
4. Government policy and intervention in tourism.
5. Potential impacts of tourism on the host community.
6. Host population acceptance of tourism.
7. Accessibility of the destination.
8. Availability of complementary infrastructure and superstructure.
questions.d: Supply-side variables may constrain or foster tourism development, even though supply should be demand-driven.
questions.w: List the factors from the slides and explain one or two briefly.

questions.q: Differentiate between travel facilitators and resistance factors, giving examples.
questions.a:
Travel facilitators predict whether a person is able to travel: disposable income, discretionary leisure time, basic tourism services and facilities, political stability, accepted mediums of exchange, access to travel documents.
Resistance factors dissuade a person from travelling: political instability and safety, the destination's location, cost of travel, health and safety issues, climate, perceived image, lack of amenities, lack of information.
questions.d: Factors affecting demand: facilitators, resistance factors and motivators.
questions.w: Facilitators make travel possible; resistance factors push people away.

questions.q: Explain the travel motivators given by Ramumbo and by Gray.
questions.a:
Ramumbo's four motivators:
1. Physical: bodily health and stress relief through physical activity.
2. Cultural: learning about other countries, cultures, arts and traditions.
3. Interpersonal: meeting new people, socialising or escaping reality.
4. Status and prestige: esteem, recognition and self-worth.
Gray: the main motive is to escape everyday routine, made of two forces:
- Wanderlust: exchanging the known for the unknown and exploring new places.
- Sunlust: seeking better physical conditions, e.g. sun and sand.
questions.d: Travel motivation: the reasons why people travel when there is often no need to do so.
questions.w: Present both theories separately and give an example for each motivator.
